items: The new Images page shows every image on your worker hosts: which ones pipelines need, which ones they build, and which can be removed.
A pipeline lists the images it builds under images: and says how many tags to keep, so old versions can be pruned safely.
gitman admin images list, missing, prune and remove manage them from the command line. Prune and remove only preview unless you add --confirm.
Workers keep the Docker build cache to 3 GiB and 7 days by default, so it no longer grows until the disk is full.
The Gitman image is built on Alpine and is about a third of the size.
A repository's Settings page has a Maintenance tab showing its disk use and running git gc.
Your account page lists every signed-in browser and lets you sign any of them out. Admins get a Sessions page.
gitman doctor checks configuration, disk space, the database, Docker and workers without changing anything.
Commits is a section of its own: the commits of a branch, tag or revision, filterable to a path from the file browser.
Gitman keeps its data in PostgreSQL, so any number of workers can run, and each repository is open to everyone signed in or limited to named readers and admins.
Ref rules decide who may push, force-push or delete, and whether a push runs a pipeline, deploys, gets secrets or gets Docker.
Pipelines live in .gitman.yml: steps run in containers, targets follow branch or tag patterns, and steps can be conditional or require images on the host.
Any branch or tag can be run by hand, a file or directory shows its history, and Gitman says why a push started no run or why a run is waiting.
The interface is redesigned and updates live, with a command palette and a no-script Jump to page.
SSH access, collaborators, self-registration, artifacts and caches are gone; use readers and ref rules instead, and archive downloads are paused for now.
No user-facing changes in this release.
No user-facing changes in this release.
Access tokens can be read-only or read-and-write, expire on a set date, and show when they were last used.
A security activity page records sign-ins, people, SSH keys, repositories and collaborators without ever showing a secret.
When Gitman is busy, Git requests wait with a clear retry time instead of hanging, and large repositories and diffs stay responsive.
Admins can see worker health and queue depth, and storage limits keep the host from filling up.
A pipeline run can be retried.
Repeated failed sign-ins are slowed down, and only the owner can change a repository's settings.
A repository is one interface: files, source navigation, commits and pipeline runs share the same pages.
A commit shows its diff, and a pipeline run shows each step and its log.
A run is tied to the exact commit that started it, even after a restart.
Large diffs are limited so a page stays usable.
The first build of the beta 17 work: pipeline runs you can inspect, commit diffs and one repository view; beta 17 replaced it the same day.
Queued runs survive a restart and keep their order.
A repository's settings page can change its description and whether it is private, and deleting a repository asks for confirmation.
Invalid settings are rejected at startup instead of failing later.
Adding an SSH key rejects invalid keys and duplicates.
A pipeline can trust a pattern of branches or tags, such as v* or release/*, instead of listing each one.
The web interface has a new design.
A failed pipeline's log says why it failed.
Gitman's Docker image now uses Debian as its base.
A pipeline run's full log can be downloaded.
The browser tab shows a Gitman icon.
Ref rules decide which branches and tags may start a pipeline, and a newer push cancels older queued runs for the same ref.
gitman version prints the version you are running.
Signing in and pushing over HTTP are safer, pushes have a size limit, and a source archive refuses unsafe files.
No user-facing changes in this release.
A pipeline can use the host's Docker daemon to build images when an admin allows it.
Gitman starts cleanly when the database is briefly busy.
A run's log keeps its place while it refreshes.
Self-hosted pipeline runs work reliably again.
Pipelines are written in YAML and run in containers instead of as scripts on the host.
An admin can set Gitman's public URL.
Signing in, sessions and signing out are safer, and long Git pushes and clones no longer time out.
Backups are consistent and safe to restore.
A run can be recovered after a worker stops without running the same work twice.
Tags can be browsed in the web interface, like branches.
Archives of branches and tags whose names contain a slash download correctly.
Passwords must be at least eight characters, and SSH keys are checked when added.
Expired sessions end instead of lingering.
Pipeline artifacts have size limits, and each run is claimed once so it cannot run twice.
The Docker image can serve Git over HTTP, so a Docker install can push and pull without extra setup.
No user-facing changes in this release.
Gitman is no longer published for Windows; releases continue for Linux and macOS.
An admin can let people create their own accounts instead of making each one.
A repository's webhook secret lets its Git host start a pipeline on push without storing a personal token.
A run's page lists the artifacts it produced.
Gitman hosts your Git repositories: browse files and commits in the browser, download an archive, and push or pull over HTTP or SSH.
People sign in with an account, and a repository can be shared with collaborators.
Access tokens let a script or Git client sign in without a password.
A push can start a pipeline on a worker, with secrets and artifacts managed from the web interface.
gitman admin manages people, repositories and backups from the command line.
